title: The application of chatbot as an L2 writing practice tool
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether chatbot-based writing practice can improve second language (L2) English writing performance among young learners and how learners perceive the chatbot as a learning tool. The study is motivated by the limited empirical evidence on long-term classroom use of chatbots for language learning, especially for productive skills such as writing. The authors focus on whether a chatbot can provide beneficial additional practice beyond traditional teacher-led writing activities.

The intervention was a scenario-based English writing chatbot built by the researchers using Google Dialogflow and populated with expressions from a fifth-grade Korean elementary school English textbook. Over 15 weeks, the experimental group used the chatbot for individual text-chat writing practice for about 10-15 minutes at the end of class, 10 times total, while the control group received traditional writing practice using the same textbook expressions through non-chatbot activities such as blanks, sentence completion, and sentence writing. The chatbot interface was constrained rather than open-ended: it used controlled dialogue scenarios tied to five textbook chapters and target expressions. Teachers minimized intervention during chatbot use except for technical issues.

Participants were 75 fifth-grade students in South Korea from two intact classes taught by the same teacher. The classes were assigned to control and experimental conditions, with students aged 10-11. Writing performance was measured with pretest and posttest timed writing tasks scored holistically by trained raters, and the experimental group also completed a perception survey with Likert-scale and open-ended items.

The main conclusion is that students who received chatbot-based writing practice performed significantly better on the posttest than those receiving traditional instruction, even when controlling for pretest scores through ANCOVA. Students also generally viewed the chatbot as useful for reviewing what they learned and appreciated practicing without embarrassment or fear of judgment. For implementation, the evidence supports a teacher-mediated classroom supplement model with short, repeated, constrained chatbot interactions rather than autonomous open use. The paper suggests affective benefits and additional practice opportunities as likely mechanisms, but links between specific implementation features and outcomes are mostly interpretive hypotheses rather than demonstrated moderators.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a school-based comparative intervention study with random allocation of two intact classes, pre/post testing, same teacher and textbook across groups, and ANCOVA controlling for baseline. However, it is a small single-site study with limited reporting, non-counterbalanced writing prompts, and no standardized effect size, so it falls short of blue-tier evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: The study shows a statistically significant positive literacy effect for an elementary EFL population, but the magnitude is unclear because no standardized effect size is reported and the outcome measure is a brief researcher-developed 3-point writing assessment. Social-emotional findings are also positive but modest and self-reported, making overall impact promising yet uncertain.

interventions.use_case: Scenario-based chatbot for elementary EFL learners to practice textbook-aligned English writing/dialogue expressions through individual text-chat writing tasks during class over 15 weeks.

Software-delivered structured writing practice via a Dialogflow-built chatbot with manually encoded textbook expressions and limited teacher intervention, compared against traditional teacher-led writing drills.

finding.finding_summary: In a 15-week comparison with Korean fifth graders, the chatbot-writing group (n=37) outperformed the teacher-led control group (n=38) on a posttest of English writing scored with a 3-point holistic rubric. Pretest scores did not differ significantly (control M=2.42, SD=0.60; experimental M=2.30, SD=0.74; U=653.00, p=.56), while posttest scores favored the chatbot group (experimental M=2.11, SD=0.61 vs. control M=1.74, SD=0.76; U=876.50, p<.05); ANCOVA controlling for pretest also showed a significant treatment effect (F=7.014, p=.010), with adjusted posttest means of 2.13 vs. 1.72.
finding.measure: Holistic L2 English writing test scores on pre/post paragraph-writing tasks using a 3-point rubric covering content, vocabulary, grammar, and mechanics
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CI for adjusted posttest means: control [1.503, 1.934], experimental [1.909, 2.346]
finding.std_deviation: Pretest SDs: control 0.60, experimental 0.74; posttest SDs: control 0.76, experimental 0.61

finding.finding_summary: Survey responses from the experimental group (n=37) suggested generally positive perceptions of the chatbot as a low-anxiety writing practice tool. Students reported that the chatbot was helpful for reviewing school learning (M=3.54/5, SD=0.96), felt somewhat comfortable conversing with it (M=3.19, SD=1.20), reported low nervousness (M=2.14, SD=1.34), and 37.84% said they would use it because it was not embarrassing to make mistakes; however, comfort and perceived writing improvement remained only moderate rather than strongly positive.
finding.measure: Student self-report survey on comfort, nervousness, usefulness, and future willingness to use chatbot writing practice
